# C10 Dossier: Signed-Off (fixed-price, AI-native nuclear engineering house; acquire the audit, automate the work)

Pool P038, researched 2026-10-18. Evidence tags: [V] primary source read this session; [S] secondary, aggregator or search snippet only; [I] my inference or arithmetic.

## 1. Bottom line

- The money is real but the idea's own market number is not sourced. NEI's 2025 capex figure is now verified. The $1.1-1.4B "outsourced engineering" pool is still an assumption, and my headcount cross-check puts it at the high end (about $0.7-1.2B today) [I].
- The proposed wedge (50.59 work) is tiny: about 3 full evaluations per plant per year.
- The "QA accountability" premise is half wrong. Appendix B leaves the licensee responsible, and AI vendors already sell to licensee engineers.
- The acquire-and-automate thesis is already under way. Pelican's nuclear-dedicated fund owns or backs GSE Solutions, EXCEL Services and Everstar (AI licensing drafting). Arlington (Enercon) and New Mountain (Jensen Hughes) set the price of acquisition targets.
- My view: median outcome is $25-45M revenue by year 6. Reaching $100M needs five hard conditions (Section 8) to hold together; I put that at roughly 5-10% [I]. It is the best idea in the pool and still wounded.

## 2. Market, bottom-up

Industry metrics: revenue per head, utilization, EBITDA margin, approved-supplier and customer count, backlog.

**Verified anchors.** NEI's August 2026 cost report (EUCG data): total cost $36.46/MWh (+5.1%); capital $7.59B vs $6.10B in 2024; labor about $8.8B; uprate capex $365M in 2025 vs $66M in 2022 but $3.3B at the 2012 peak; regulatory capex $270M vs a $2.66B peak in 2014. NEI attributes the 2025 capital rise "largely" to inflation plus life-extension upgrades, and capital cost is still 36.4% below 2012 [V] ([NEI](https://www.nei.org/getContentAsset/47fa8caa-9b0d-4029-932c-07f902e82f4f/8d8ff8d6-b2ae-401b-a63c-f6b108e809d2/2024-Costs-in-Context-final.pdf?language=en-US)). So "capex +24%" is a rebound from a trough, not a record engineering wave.

**Outsourced engineering pool: no published figure found.** Three triangulations:
- The idea's assumption (10% of capital plus 5% of non-labor opex) gives about $1.1B [I].
- Supplier revenue: Enercon, which says it supports about 90% of US plants, shows about $210M in aggregator data and $220M in a 2012 company case study [S] ([Prospeo](https://prospeo.io/c/enercon-services), [Great Game](https://www.greatgame.com/resources/case-studies/topic/oil-gas-chemicals)). Sargent & Lundy (S&L) revenue is undisclosed. A boutique, DP Engineering, had $20M+ revenue and about 110 staff [V] ([SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/944480/000094448019000006/exh99-2.htm)).
- Headcount: operating-plant engineers are 6,900-7,400 FTE in 2025, rising to 9,200-10,400 by 2030 [V] ([NCEA/USC](https://energyanalytics.org/nuclear-workforce/)). At $120-180k revenue per supplier head, $1.1B implies 6,000-9,000 outsourced engineers, nearly as many as in-house. That is plausible only if licensing consultants and design houses are counted, so I use $0.7-1.2B for 2026 and $1.0-1.6B by 2030 [I].

**Payers x spend [I].** About 25 owners and 55 sites. At $0.9B, that is about $16M of outsourced engineering per site per year. $100M is about 8-14% of today's pool (6-10% of the 2030 pool), or $1.8M from every site. Ten single-site operators at 20% share give $15-35M. Beyond that you must displace multi-year "engineer of choice" alliances: Exelon-S&L covered 17 units (2002, current status unverified) ([Power Eng](https://www.power-eng.com/nuclear/sargent-lundy-signs-engineer-of-choice-contract-for-exelons-nuclear-and-fossil-fleets/)), and TVA moved most nuclear design to S&L in 2006 [S] ([Power Eng](https://www.power-eng.com/nuclear/sargent-lundy-selected-for-tva-nuclear-plants/)).

**The 50.59 wedge does not pay.** Wolf Creek filed six full 50.59 evaluations in 2017-18 [V] ([NRC](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML1908/ML19086A114.pdf)); Callaway reported four across May 2016-Dec 2017 [S] ([NRC](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML1815/ML18158A557.pdf)). That is about 3 per plant per year, or 150-300 fleet-wide; at $30-50k each, under $15M [I]. Screenings are more numerous but low value. This is a quality-proof pilot, not revenue. Real volume sits in calculations, design changes and project engineering; I found no hours or cost data for those.

**Timing.** Vistra says most uprate growth capital falls after 2028 [S] ([Yahoo](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/vistra-corp-q4-2025-earnings-010956189.html)). Crane restart is targeted for 2027 and Duane Arnold for 2029 [S] ([ANS](https://www.ans.org/news/2025-10-28/article-7501/nextera-and-google-ink-a-deal-to-restart-duane-arnold/)).

## 3. Competitors

| Competitor | Type | Verified facts | Threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enercon/Pond | Hourly firm turned PE platform | Arlington bought it from Oaktree (Apr 2026); 2,700+ staff combined; "additional add-ons planned"; reported $1.25B equity, unconfirmed [V] ([Arlington](https://arlingtoncap.com/news/arlington-capital-partners-acquires-enercon-and-completes-merger-with-its-portfolio-company-pond/)) | High: same targets, fresh capital, same customers |

**Free and in-house substitutes.** DOE/INL/Argonne run AI-drafting work in the open. Owners' own 6,900-7,400 engineers, equipped with Nuclearn, Atomic Canyon or Westinghouse tools, are the real substitute: every point of productivity they gain shrinks overflow demand [I]. Utilities Service Alliance already contracts procurement-engineering services for members [S] ([USA Inc.](https://usainc.org/?p=2983)).

**Not found:** any startup selling fixed-price, AI-produced Appendix B deliverables. The white space is real but narrow. AI-enabled services roll-ups exist elsewhere (Thrive Holdings is reportedly raising $2B for accounting/IT; General Catalyst earmarked $1.5B) but I found no engineering example [S] ([PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/?p=3926838)). Critics argue acquired legacy pricing, workflows and client relationships resist change [S] ([Emcap](https://emcap.substack.com/p/the-ai-roll-up-trap)).

**Moat view.** S&L: switching costs, intangibles and scale all strong. Enercon/Pond: moderate-strong. Pelican platform: moderate. Signed-Off at launch: weak on all four; by year 5 only moderate switching costs (listed status, accepted per-plant templates) [I].

**Gate claims re-checked.** Confirmed: Enercon/Arlington, Nuclearn's $10.5M round, the DOE-Everstar test, Pelican's stakes. Corrected: NEI's 2025 capital figure ($7.59B) is now verified; Enercon revenue is about $210-220M from weak sources; Nuclearn's reactor count varies 50-70+ by source; "approval takes 12-24 months" has no source (NUPIC shows a 33-month cycle and a five-customer minimum); The Nuclear Company's funding ranges $46M-$138M across aggregators. New since the gate: Pelican's integrated platform, New Mountain-Jensen Hughes, EnergySolutions-WMG, the roughly 3-per-year 50.59 volume, Part 21's reach to engineering services, AI exclusions in E&O, and the INL case study.

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

For: owners outsource design under multi-year alliances (above); one major utility awarded GSE a $35M/2-year staff-augmentation master agreement in 2020 [S] ([Staffing Industry](https://www.staffingindustry.com/Editorial/Industrial-Staffing-Report/Dec.-17-2020/Contract-watch-GSE-Systems-awarded-two-master-services-agreements)); AtkinsRéalis-FANCO is up to CAD 250M (US$181M) over five years [S] ([NEI Mag](https://www.neimagazine.com/news/fanco-atkinsrealis-forge-alliance/)); PE paying a reported $1.25B of equity for Enercon.

Against or missing: I found no RFP, tender or owner statement asking for fixed-price AI-produced deliverables. MIT Technology Review's uprate story names price and equipment, not engineer shortage, as the constraint [V] ([MIT TR](http://www.technologyreview.com/2026/10/15/1146577/nuclear-power-upgrade)). Shortage data is workforce-level (IEA, USC), not overflow-demand-level.

## 5. Unit economics and capital

- **Rates.** One S&L 2022 invoice in a Texas filing shows $102-$270/hr from Associate I to Principal [S] ([PUC](https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/56211_218_1394038.PDF)). At about $160-200 blended and 1,500 billable hours, that is $240-300k per billable engineer. Actual all-in revenue per head: DP Engineering about $180k, Enercon about $120k [V/S]. So "400 engineers at $250k" understates staffing: about 450-560 total staff at today's productivity (rate model vs DP Engineering actuals; Enercon's ratio implies more) [I].
- **Margins.** DP Engineering's earn-out EBITDA thresholds ($2.75-4.3M on $20M+) imply 13-21% [V/I]; consulting firms generally run low-to-mid 20s% [S] ([Chaffe](https://www.bvresources.com/articles/bvwire/consulting-firm-multiples-climb-with-size-per-chaffe-analysis)).
- **AI lever [I].** Assume 30% fewer hours per deliverable and a 15% price cut: revenue per hour worked rises about 21% ($200 to $243). $100M then needs about 370-410 staff instead of 450-500 (rate model). That is a few EBITDA points, available to any rival using the same models, and independent verification (Criterion III) does not compress.
- **Capital.** DP Engineering sold in 2019 for $13.5M cash plus up to $5M earn-out (about 0.7x revenue upfront) [V]. 2026 pricing is higher: lower-middle-market engineering 4-8x EBITDA, specialists 9-12x [S] ([CT Acquisitions](https://ctacquisitions.com/?p=15590)); technical services index 12.5x in Q1 2026 [S] ([Investec](https://www.investec.com/advisory?p=58126)). Reaching $100M by acquisition at about 1.0-1.5x revenue is $60-120M plus working capital: PE-scale, not founder-scale [I]. Pilot plus a software-QA plan is low seven figures [I, unsourced].

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **Appendix B** [V] ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-50/appendix-Appendix%20B%20to%20Part%2050)): the licensee "shall retain responsibility" for the QA program (Criterion I); design checking must be by people other than the original designers (III); the licensee assesses supplier effectiveness at intervals (VII). A supplier cannot absorb the owner's accountability; it sells process comfort.
- **Part 21** [V] ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-21/section-21.3)): "basic component" includes safety-related design, analysis and consulting services, so suppliers carry defect-evaluation and reporting duties.
- **AI.** No NRC rule for licensee AI use was found; DOE proposes an NRC working group [V]. Whether an AI tool in a human-verified workflow needs NQA-1 Subpart 2.7 software QA is unresolved in my sources. If not required, the QA moat is moot; if required, no vendor claims it [I].
- **Approved-supplier path.** NUPIC audits need a supplier with at least five NRC-licensee customers; the standard cycle is 33 months [V] ([NUPIC](https://www.nupic.com)). I found no source for the idea's "12-24 months." A greenfield entrant is in a catch-22, which is why acquisition is the route. Rebuilding an acquired firm's QA program and tools may trigger customer re-acceptance [I]. NEI 22-04 Rev 1 (Aug 2026) would let ISO 9001 suppliers serve safety-related work because NQA-1 suppliers are shrinking [S] ([NRC](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML2621/ML26219A186.pdf)); helpful for scarcity now, erodes it if approved (aimed at components).
- **Professional licensure.** NSPE says reviewing documents after preparation, without involvement in design, does not meet "responsible charge" [S] ([NSPE](https://nspe.org/node/25565)). Where state PE seals apply, AI-drafts-human-reviews is legally weaker.
- **Insurance.** ISO generative-AI exclusion endorsements took effect Jan 1, 2026 and some carriers exclude AI claims from E&O [S] ([Jenner](https://www.jenner.com/en/news-insights/publications/in-law360-partner-david-kroeger-examines-emerging-ai-insurance-exclusions)); no policy text seen. A fixed-price, rework-guaranteed AI house may carry uninsured risk. Price-Anderson (to 2065) covers nuclear-incident claims, not contract or rework losses [S] ([Morgan Lewis](https://www.morganlewis.com/blogs/upandatom/2024/04/congress-gives-40-year-extension-for-price-anderson-nuclear-liability-framework)).

## 7. Is the why-now real?

Partly. Real: restarts, $4.3B of Constellation uprates, DOE loans, thin engineer pipeline (about 15,400 nuclear engineers nationally, median wage $135,760 [V]). Overstated: the drafting speedup is public (INL, DOE) and open to all; DOE's roadmap is closing the "unowned AI output" gap; incumbents are buying AI and capital. A first-mover window is 12-24 months at most [I].

## 8. Do the upside assumptions hold?

| Assumption | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| a. Buy an approved boutique in year 1 | DP Engineering comp; but Arlington, Pelican and New Mountain have add-on mandates | Plausible, price contested |
| b. AI removes 40%+ of hours on bounded deliverables | INL 2026 case study: experts estimated about 50% savings on a safety-document chapter, but found hallucinations, missing parameters and AI artifacts, on gpt-4o; "acceptable first draft" [V] ([INL](https://nric.inl.gov/content/uploads/34/2026/07/RPT-26-90824-Rev-0-Evaluation-of-AI-Enabled-Digital-Documented-Safety-Analysis-A-Case-Study.pdf)). DOE test is drafting-only with no error count. Westinghouse claims 25%. No data on calculations or design changes | Unproven; credible only for drafting-heavy work |
| c. 5+ owner QA groups accept software QA in 24 months | No precedent found; EPRI/INPO's NIVA pilot slides mark output "UNVERIFIED" [S] ([EPRI](https://restservice.epri.com/publicattachment/97144)) | Unproven |
| d. Hire about 250 engineers | Really about 370-560 staff; S&L alone grew 14.5% | Hard |
| e. Developer and restart licensing adds $25-35M | Developers award engineering to exclusive EPC alliances (AtkinsRéalis-FANCO; Hyundai-TerraPower [S] ([Neutron Bytes](https://neutronbytes.com/2026/08/14/terrapower-signs-hyundai-as-epc-for-eight-natrium-reactors/))); Everstar and EXCEL own the AI-licensing angle | Likely $10-20M as a subcontractor |
| f. Incumbents do not match for 3+ years | S&L AI hire, Westinghouse CMIS, Pelican portfolio, Enercon capital | Unlikely to hold |

## 9. Synthesis

Scenarios [I]: Bull 10% (requires b through f together; $100M+ by year 7). Base 40-45% (roll up two or three boutiques, a handful of owners, $25-45M). Bear 45-50% (stalls under $15M or is absorbed by Pelican/Enercon).

Durable advantage: approved-supplier listing plus accepted per-plant templates (moderate switching costs). Structural vulnerabilities: services margins; a commoditizing AI edge; owners keep the liability so will not pay a premium for "accountability"; E&O insurability. Current state is early and contested.

What would change my mind: one owner signing a multi-year fixed-price deliverable contract; NRC or EPRI language that independently verified AI output needs no separate tool QA; a qualified boutique available below 6x EBITDA.

Cheapest next test (2-3 months): interview 10 design-engineering directors on percent outsourced, appetite for per-deliverable pricing, and whether their QA group would require NQA-1 on the tool; run one paid calculation-revision pilot with the owner's engineer verifying; get E&O quotes with AI use disclosed; ask a broker for 2-3 boutique targets and valuations. Founder fit: this needs a credentialed nuclear QA and licensing insider plus institutional capital.

**Unverified:** outsourced-engineering pool; S&L and Enercon revenue; per-plant calculation and design-change volume; E&O policy text; NRC licensee AI guidance; Nuclearn's NRC deck and the Axios Atomic Canyon piece (403 on fetch; snippet only).

objections: The exact model already exists at the target scale, with deeper capital, and micro-tier entrants sit on the same channel. HomeServe Deutschland (a Brookfield portfolio company) buys SHK and electrical firms, keeps their names, leaves management in place and centralises admin, digital, purchasing and recruiting. It went from 8 firms at the start of 2024 to 21 by March 2025 and 24 firms with about 1,300 staff by Oct 2025. German revenue was reportedly about EUR 50M in 2023 and about EUR 100M in 2024, which is the $100M milestone the idea is aiming for. In Mar 2026 it bought Scheer (about 50 staff) with the stated plan of 'long-term growth with the existing management team'. Around it: VINCI Energies agreed to buy R+S Group (EUR 191M revenue, 1,200 staff, electrical/HVAC) in 2025; Konzmann/KLAR (21 firms, about EUR 180M); Builtech/VDK (about EUR 2B, 150+ businesses). At the sub-EUR 2M tier, MEISTEREHRE (founded by an SHK Meister and a Betriebswirt) is advertising for firms with 5-20 staff in Altbayern on the HWK Muenchen Betriebsboerse, the same chamber channel and region as the idea's first-10-deals wedge. SHK Group/SHK Ventures (Berlin) buys micro firms, leaves the owner as Geschaeftsfuehrer, and offers back office. If this entrant gets traction, the response is cheap: HomeServe or VINCI lower their size floor or raise the cash bid, using reference sellers, existing back office and Brookfield or VINCI cost of capital against a EUR 15M seed.

The 'recurring statutory service' thesis points the platform at segments where the strongest incumbents are OEMs and funded consolidators, or where the claimed Meister moat does not exist. HwO Anlage A (53 trades) has no lift or fire-protection trade. Only Elektrotechniker (no. 25) and Installateur/Heizungsbauer (no. 24) are gated, and those are the two trades with no evidence on recurring share. DGUV V3 testing may be done by any 'zur Pruefung befaehigte Person' (electrotechnical training plus about a year of experience) or by a specialised provider, so in-house staff and testing firms compete without a Meister. Lifts: Schindler bought three firms of 10, 14 and 25 staff in 2023 and says small firms merging into larger ones is a trend. TKE kept buying in 2026 despite the Kone deal. Kone advertises brand-independent maintenance. The Kone-TKE merger (EUR 29.4B, closing no earlier than Q2 2027) is expected to put European service assets up for sale, possibly to a financial investor. Fire: Waterland's Wtech made its first German add-on (Feuerfuchs) in Apr 2026, and svt/Ergon already has 1,500+ staff. For SHK, Thermondo, Enpal and 1Komma5 sell service contracts at installation, and OEM warranties require annual servicing, so the recurring base is being intermediated. The Elektro trade itself is shrinking: ZVEH reported Elektrotechniker revenue down 4.8% in 2024.

The size floor incumbents respect is structural, not an oversight. PE and groups target about 20 staff and EUR 2M+ revenue because a Betriebsleiter and holding costs cannot be carried by a EUR 0.8-2M firm. Konzmann's own Q1 2026 report shows the economics of the best-documented comp: Q1 revenue EUR 29.7M (down from 31.7M), EBITDA adjusted 3.9% and EBITA adjusted 2.3% of total output (seasonally weakest quarter), LTM EBITDA about EUR 19.6M, net debt EUR 66.9M at FY25 (leverage 3.0x, 3.7x pro forma), a EUR 85M bond, LTM interest paid EUR 6.7M (about a third of EBITDA), trade working capital EUR 32M. Electrical solutions are only EUR 10.4M of a EUR 148.5M backlog, so this is project-heavy TGA, not a recurring-inspection book. My arithmetic: a Meister costs about EUR 53-63k gross (median salary snippets), so about EUR 64-76k with an assumed 21% on-costs, or 4.3-5.1% of EUR 1.5M revenue. That is the idea's 7.5% mid margin minus about 4.7% Betriebsleiter minus 2.5% holding cost, leaving roughly 0.3% EBIT. This weakens only if the 7.5% was already after a market-rate manager, which no source shows. Per law-firm commentary (not primary-verified), one Betriebsleiter can cover a second site only if reachable within minutes, so hub-and-spoke tuck-ins across towns each need a Meister. Larger groups spread that cost over 20-60 staff firms. The micro tier is left to Meister-founders who are their own Betriebsleiter at no marginal cost.

'Hold-forever, owner stays, central back office, Meister ladder' is the incumbents' standard pitch, so the 7 Powers counter-positioning claim fails. Counter-positioning needs rivals who cannot copy without hurting themselves. HomeServe (names kept, owners stay, long-term), Konzmann (brochure promises to take all staff), Builtech ('reliable succession partner'), VINCI (a listed strategic that does not flip), S&V Mittelstandspartner ('no portfolio, no exit timeline') and MEISTEREHRE (Meister-run) already offer it. The rival's cost of copying is zero because they already do it. The gate's own evidence for 'strong' (Konzmann, HWP, Builtech reaching EUR 180M-2B) proves that PE-funded rivals have the revenue path, not that a hold-forever entrant can win sellers. Moreover the gate hands the entrant the same HWK Nachfolgemoderator referral channel that HWP, Builtech and Konzmann already work. The only differentiator left is a Geselle-to-Meister equity ladder, which has no German precedent found and is employed-Betriebsleiter-only.

Bid-price and cost-of-capital disadvantage against strategics and subsidised individuals. The idea prices at 0.4-0.6x revenue with half deferred, while sellers expect about 0.87x in Handwerk. Strategics with synergies (VINCI, HomeServe, Schindler, Kone) can pay more cash, and a Nordic bond-funded platform like Konzmann is already paying around 9% on debt. A hold-forever yield of 7-10% unlevered means leverage is negative, so the platform needs EUR 50-100M of equity. Add-ons were 71.4% of European PE buyouts in Q1 2026 (PitchBook via Nordvisory), competitive bidding reportedly lifts prices 15-30%, and unitranche debt costs 9-11% with 40-55% equity required. The alternatives for a micro seller are cheaper: an employee or local Meister successor funded by subsidised capital (NRW.BANK KBG silent partnership of EUR 25-250k to finance the purchase price for succession buyers, 10-year term; KfW 077 with 100% guarantee), a neighbouring competitor, or simply closing (about 54,000 Handwerk closures against 49,000 handovers over two years). The platform has to beat all of them on price and certainty while paying a Meister.

On 2026-09-18 a Fifth Circuit panel (Smith, Southwick, Douglas) granted Texas a stay pending appeal in Ward v. Muth, No. 26-50619. It had already administratively stayed the injunction on 9/9. Both the dossier ('no ruling as of Oct 18') and the gate ('main risk is the Fifth Circuit') treated this as an open question. The order is 7 pages and says HHSC is 'likely to succeed on the merits.' It calls the district court's use of Jackson v. Indiana 'probably inappropriate' and says substantive due process does not entitle plaintiffs to a 21-day limit. It says the waitlist 'is likely to pass [rational basis] with flying colors' and that 'HHSC must start redirecting its resources immediately' if there is no stay. The benchmarks, monitoring and four-year clock are all frozen. Without the order, the 'why now' disappears and Texas has no legal duty to buy a bed. The order is labeled preliminary and a merits panel will decide, but the first factor of the stay test is 'strong showing of likelihood of success,' so this is a bad sign for the plaintiffs. Texas also never needed the order to be a buyer: the pre-ruling waitlist was already down about 40% from its Dec 2022 peak with no new private operator involved.

THE MONEY IS GOING TO STATE-OWNED AND UNIVERSITY-OPERATED BEDS, WHICH ARE A PRICE-FREE SUBSTITUTE. HHSC's FY2028-29 request (submitted Sept 2026) protected state hospitals from the 3% cut. Coverage of the request mentions no forensic or contracted-bed ask and no cost estimate for meeting the order. The legislature has put more than $2.5B into state hospital builds since 2017, adding 680+ owned beds. Six more projects finish in 2027 (175 net new beds, 540 replaced or converted). The new 292-bed Dallas hospital is run by UT Southwestern, and the Houston, Lubbock and Amarillo hospitals are also university-linked builds. The statutes that fund contracted forensic capacity (SB 1677) name nonprofits and governmental entities, and Hays County's new jail-based program is a state grant to Hill Country MHMR, not to a private operator. A for-profit entrant is competing with the buyer's own balance sheet and with grant-funded public entities. The dossier's own number, $3.7M per state-built bed, shows the state is willing to pay far more to own capacity than a bed-day contract would cost.

THE INCUMBENTS ALREADY HOLD THE SHELLS AND THE TRACK RECORD, AND THE ASSET-LIGHT ROUTE LEAVES A NEW ENTRANT AS A JUNIOR PARTNER. Recovery Solutions (the ex-Wellpath behavioral unit, now lender-owned and debt-free) has about 3,700 staff in 70 facilities, and its website now says 12 states. It holds Florida's 446 privatized forensic beds. It won Washington's Maple Lane program through competitive procurement in 2015 and manages Montgomery County TX, where the CEO calls it the 'junior partner.' Liberty Healthcare holds the jail-based niche: Riverside County gave it a sole-source five-year contract (Jan 2024 to Dec 2028, about $2.9M a year) and San Bernardino was Liberty's earlier win. Texas requires a licensed hospital with Joint Commission accreditation for inpatient restoration, so the 'modular, 6-12 month' unit is not a sellable product. That leaves two options. Build and own at $0.5-3.7M per bed, which a startup cannot finance. Or manage someone else's shell at a thin fee, which is where Recovery Solutions already sits with a lender-owned balance sheet and no debt service. An incumbent response is trivial: it bids the same county-built shells with an existing licensed staff pool.

PRIVATE FORENSIC CAPACITY IS BOUGHT AS A TEMPORARY BRIDGE, AND BUYERS WRITE THE EXIT INTO THE CONTRACT. Washington's Trueblood settlement set a hard closure date of July 1, 2024 for the Maple Lane program, whether or not wait-time triggers were met. Closure is also tied to a median wait of 9 days or less for four consecutive months. Yakima's operator, Comprehensive Healthcare, quit mid-contract in 2021 over workforce shortages, so the operator-side failure mode is real. Colorado's April 2026 budget memo (as summarized in search results) shows 640 competency beds, of which only 84 are private contracts (about 13%) and 96 are jail-based. The decree ends 2027-12-01. Florida's DCF reportedly asked for no new forensic bed funding in its 2026-27 request despite its own gap analysis showing 2,000+ beds needed by 2029 (from a summary of a 2026 complaint, so not primary). The pattern is that states under litigation fund state builds first and rent private beds only as an interim, and the rental ends when the state's capacity opens. A five-year availability contract is exposed to this ramp-down, and 600 beds at one operator has no precedent in any of the four states.

NO ONE WANTS THIS ASSET, AND THE ECONOMICS DO NOT CLEAR EVEN IF BEDS ARE BOUGHT. Wellpath's whole behavioral unit ($425M revenue, about 3,000 patients, 20+ years) drew about 70 NDAs and no qualifying outside bid. The lenders took it for a $395M credit bid, about 0.93x revenue. Capital markets have already passed on the scaled version of this business twice. At the margins in the dossier (8-12% EBITDA, with a Texas private operator saying it loses money at a $529 rate against $700-900 cost), $100M of revenue is $8-12M of EBITDA with a hard-to-insure forensic patient cohort (the 2025 Florida wrongful-death suit is the tail risk). The cheaper jail-based and outpatient alternatives set the price anchor: Harris County at $261, Liberty San Bernardino at about $170 and Colorado jail-based at $421. The first SB 528 cost comparison in Aug 2027 gives HHSC a public benchmark to push private rates down. Texas jail-based programs restore poorly (10 of 19 restored half or fewer), so a high price needs a high-acuity inpatient product that only licensed hospitals can sell.

# C11 Dossier: P062 "Outreach Without Selling" (gate pick "Outreach Partner Labs")

Researched 2026-10-18. Method: about 50 searches and fetches, plus primary filings read directly (Quest 10-K FY2024, Labcorp 10-K FY2021, CMS manual chapter 16, 42 CFR 424.73, XiFin 2026 report, Quest Q4 2025 prepared remarks, Sonic FY26 deck). Tags: (S) sourced, (A) my arithmetic or assumption, (U) unverified. Pages that returned 403 (Business Wire, Sonic's site, GenomeWeb) were used only through search summaries and are marked "search summary".

## 1. Verdict

**Weak, trending dead as a $100M business. I would not advance it as written.**

- The pool is real and large.
- The $100M revenue figure is arithmetically reachable only as consolidated JV revenue. That revenue earns about $8-15M of EBITDA and needs roughly $120M+ of equity at the multiples national buyers actually pay (A).
- The plan fails four checks:
  - The legal structure contradicts Medicare billing rules.
  - Capital is understated by about 2x.
  - The competitor set is far bigger than "none found".
  - The closest funded precedent (RDL, $250M committed in 2012) had stalled by 2015 after backing away from deals.
- My estimate (A), 5-7 years out:

| Case | Probability | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Bear | ~50% | No controlled JV closes; 2-4 management contracts, $2-6M revenue, or a pivot to advisory |
| Base | ~35% | One JV plus a few managed systems; $35-45M revenue, $3-5M EBITDA |
| Bull | ~15% | 2-3 JVs plus 8 managed systems; $100-130M revenue, $10-15M EBITDA, $120M+ invested |

- Median is about $8-12M, below the gate's $20M. Upside is about $100M of revenue but not $100M of value creation.

## 2. Industry metrics (step 0)

Outreach runs on:
- net revenue per test or requisition
- contribution margin %
- cash collected per dollar billed
- volume growth
- sale price as a multiple of revenue

## 3. Market and bottom-up (steps 1-2)

**The pool**
- Quest's investor day sizes hospital outreach at about $20B of a $58B physician channel across "600+ health systems", with about 20 Quest deals in a decade. (S) [Quest 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000094787125000321/ss4596431_ex9901.htm)
- That is about $33M per system (A).
- Program sizes are skewed. Chi's 2016 survey had a median of $12.8M and a mean of $24.9M. Contribution margin was 23-33%, defined as revenue less dedicated and incremental outreach costs. (S) [CLP survey summary](https://clpmag.com/resource-center/research/survey-laboratory-outreach-enjoys-favorable-profitability/)
- Hospital labs were 13.6% of 6,411 PAMA reporters, about 870 NPIs. These are NPIs, not systems. (S, computed) [CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/preliminary-calendar-year-cy-2027-medicare-clinical-laboratory-fee-schedule-payment-rates)

**Flow of deals** (the real constraint)
- Quest and Labcorp closed at least 29 outreach deals from 2013 to 2024, all to the nationals, with prices undisclosed. (S) [G2 deal list](https://www.g2intelligence.com/dx-deals-outreach-deals-by-quest-labcorp-are-still-ramping-up/)
- Kaufman Hall counted about 2 transactions a year in 2013-2021 and 7 in 2022. (S) [HFMA](https://www.hfma.org/finance-and-business-strategy/healthcare-business-trends/strategic-alternatives-abound-for-health-system-outreach-laboratories/)
- Labcorp's CEO said it had 13 new or closed hospital or regional lab deals in 2025. (S, search summary) [360Dx](https://www.360dx.com/clinical-lab-management/labcorp-reaffirms-outreach-acquisitions-jpm-key-growth-cites-strong-deal)
- So roughly 5-13 systems a year decide to monetize (A). If 10-25% would pick a partner over cash (A, my assumption), 1-3 contestable systems appear a year.

**Two ways to $100M**

| Path | Math (A) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Fees | 9% of a $35M program is about $3.2M a system; $100M needs about 32 systems, about 5% of all systems | At 1-3 contestable a year, 10-30 years |
| Consolidated JV revenue | About 3 JVs at $33M | Needs the equity in section 6 |

- Verdict on the pool: size is not the problem. Velocity, capital and win rate against cash buyers are.

## 4. Competitors: gate claims tested (steps 4-8)

**Confirmed**
- Quest Co-Lab:
  - Revenue grew from about $300M (2019) to $800M (2024). (S) Same investor day deck.
  - The Corewell JV is 51/49, covering 21 hospitals, with a new lab due Q1 2027. (S) [press release](https://s2.q4cdn.com/390454341/files/doc_news/Corewell-Health-and-Quest-Diagnostics-Complete-Laboratory-Joint-Venture-Transaction-in-Michigan-2026.pdf)
  - Quest's own pitch: "Hospitals value our flexible solutions for accessing expertise, innovation and capital." (S) [Q4 2025 remarks](https://s2.q4cdn.com/390454341/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/Quest-Diagnostics-2025-Q4-Year-End-Webcast-Script.pdf) This is the startup's pitch, from a bigger and better-funded seller.
- Labcorp:
  - It bought CHS for $195M and has Parkview pending. (S) [Labcorp](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/press-releases/community-health-systems-announces-definitive-agreement-sell), [MedTech Dive](https://www.medtechdive.com/news/Labcorp-deal-Parkview-Health-outreach-lab-assets/805514/)
- Sonic USA:
  - It is flat on organic growth, and its operating review is ongoing. (S) [Sonic FY26](https://announcements.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20260820/pdf/072zhg5rhzbt79.pdf)
  - It has hospital JVs such as ProMedica, where over 90% of testing is done at the JV core lab. (S, search summary) [Sonic](https://www.sonichealthcareusa.com/about-us/news/promedica-health-system-in-new-joint-venture-partnership/)
- ARUP and Mayo are free or cheap advisory substitutes. ARUP offers an outreach-value assessment. (S) [ARUP](https://www.aruplab.com/magnify26/commercial-laboratories-want-buy-your-lab-operations-heres-why-math-not-your-favor)
- Consultants: Chi Solutions, owned by PE-created Accumen, which sells shared-savings partnerships. (S) [Dark Report](https://www.darkintelligencegroup.com/the-dark-report/laboratory-management/accumen-acquires-chi-to-beef-up-lab-consulting/)

**Refuted or changed**
- "No independent operator runs the commercial half."
  - **Orion Laboratories and FMOL Health.** In January 2026 they announced a JV in Louisiana. Orion is described as the state's largest independent lab and contributes operations, technology and logistics. FMOL had been using Labcorp. Terms are undisclosed. (S) [Healthcare Journal BR](https://www.healthcarejournalbr.com/node/3348), [Business Report](https://www.businessreport.com/business/orion-labs-fmol-health-partner-to-expand-services-across-the-state)
  - **TriCore.** It is hospital-owned and runs lab management for other systems, such as Lovelace. (S) [TriCore](https://www.tricore.org/lovelace-health-system-selects-tricore/)
  - **Atalan.** Froedtert's WDL launched this with HealthEco in 2023 as a hospital-lab network. I found no member list or update. (S) [MLO](https://www.mlo-online.com/management/article/53074544/froedtert-health-wisconsin-diagnostic-laboratories-and-healtheco-launch-atalan)
  - **Mednet Services.** It was an older "direct and network-based outreach" operator partnered with ARUP. Current status unknown. (S) [BioSpace](https://www.biospace.com/arup-laboratories-signs-agreement-with-b-mednet-services-b-to-expand-its-outreach-services)
- PAML as the "independent operator":
  - It was owned by Providence and CHI, with about $300M of revenue and 1,600 staff when sold to Labcorp. (S) [Lund Report](https://www.thelundreport.org/content/paml-announces-sale-labcorp), [Labcorp](https://www.labcorp.com/labcorp-acquire-pathology-associates-medical-laboratories-providence-health-services-and-catholic)
  - Its end state was a sale by its hospital owners, not an independent success.

**In-house substitutes**
- Tucson Medical Center took outreach back after selling it in 2003. Bryan Health built its own program. (S) [ARUP](https://www.aruplab.com/magnify26/commercial-laboratories-want-buy-your-lab-operations-heres-why-math-not-your-favor)
- Kootenai Health had a PAML JV with a 50/50 revenue split. PAML ran preanalytics and billing while Kootenai tested. Labcorp bought PAML in 2017 and converted it into a testing agreement with a 5-year noncompete. Kootenai says it was "losing money", insourced in 2022 with Mayo Outreach Insights, and reports EBIDA up about $10M from FY2022 to FY2024. (S) [CAP Today](https://www.captodayonline.com/how-a-core-lab-took-back-its-outpatient-business/)
  - This is the best published case of this exact model. The operator took half the revenue, the sponsor was acquired and changed the terms, and the hospital left.

**Software:** MEDITECH outreach portal, hc1 and similar tools are commodity enablers, not competitors. (U)

## 5. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Positive**
- Hospitals do pay for outside lab operations: Quest's Co-Lab grew about 22% a year.
- The JV template is accepted: Corewell, FMOL/Orion, ProMedica.
- Distress is real:
  - Median health-system margin was -0.6% in January 2026 (Strata via ARUP). (S)
  - 43.5% of 2025 healthcare M&A involved a distressed party. (S)
  - Labcorp's CEO says Medicaid cuts and the end of ACA subsidies may push systems to sell. (S, search summary)
- Outreach billing is bad:
  - For hospital outreach, "procedure not paid separately" was 61.2% of denials and duplicates 22.6%.
  - Appeals recover 0.03% of receipts at $48 each. (S) [XiFin 2026](https://media.xifin.com/prod/uploads/EWC-2026-XiFin-2026-Payor-Denial-Impact-Report.pdf)

**Negative**
- Every one of the 29+ listed outreach exits went to Quest or Labcorp. I found no US case of a system choosing a venture-backed operator over cash.
- I found no open RFP for an outreach operating partner (search limited to public web).
- Sellers skew distressed, and distressed sellers want cash, not a 49% stake:
  - Jefferson sold its lab business for $108M against $231M of operating loss (FY2023).
  - Tufts cut about 600 jobs after its sale.
  - CHS was pruning non-core assets. (S) [Becker's](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/jefferson-sells-lab-business-for-108m/), [Digital Health News](https://www.digitalhealthnews.com/chs-completes-194m-sale-of-outpatient-lab-assets-to-labcorp)
- The signer is the CFO. Budget exists in the sense that outreach P&L exists, but the alternative on the table is a check.

## 6. Unit economics and capital

**National analogs**

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Quest 2025 adjusted operating margin | 15.9% (S) [8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000102207926000005/dgx123120258-kexhibit991.htm) |
| Quest Corewell Co-Lab | About $250M of 2026 revenue "at low single-digit margins" (S, Q4 2025 remarks) |
| Labcorp on outreach acquisitions | Margins "typically lower than the company average early on" (S) [MedTech Dive](https://www.medtechdive.com/news/labcorp-buys-baystate-health-outreach-lab/695687/) |

- A scaled, synergy-rich national earns 16%. Management-type revenue earns a few points. A startup does not beat that.

**Prices paid**
- Ascension: $400M for assets with about $150M of annual revenue, or 2.7x. (S) [Labcorp release](https://labcorp.com/labcorp-announces-2021-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-results), [10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/920148/000092014822000015/lh-20211231.htm)
- The gate cites BioReference at 2.4x (not re-verified by me).
- Quest's 2024 outreach buys were $230M, $200M and $183M. Revenue was undisclosed. (S) [Quest 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1022079/000102207925000044/dgx-20241231.htm)
- Conflict to note: MedTech Dive says Quest paid "$2.2B" for outreach. The 10-K says $2.2B is the aggregate for all 2024 deals, including LifeLabs at about US$1B. The three outreach buys total $613M.

**Capital (A)**
- At 2.4-2.7x, a 51% stake in $100M of outreach revenue costs about $122-138M. The gate assumed $50-90M at 1.0-1.3x.
- Nationals can pay that because they cut costs by moving testing into their own hubs. Labcorp expected to "return its cost of capital by year two" on Ascension.
- A standalone operator cannot. At an 8-15% margin, $100M of revenue is worth $80-180M at 10-12x EBITDA (A), against $122-138M paid for 51% of it.
- RDL's CEO said the same thing in 2015: hospital lab payment levels differed from independent-lab levels, prices exceeded likely value, and RDL backed away from deals. (S) [G2](https://g2intelligence.com/?p=1172)

**Hospital's side of the fee (A)**
- A $33M program at 25% contribution is $8.3M.
- A 9% fee is $3.0M, or 36% of that contribution.
- The hospital's savings pool is 10-20% of addressable costs on vendor claims (Quest/Kaufman Hall). On about $25M of direct cost that is $2.5-5.0M. The fee consumes 60-120% of it.
- Selling at 2.7x pays about 10.7 years of contribution up front.
- Cost benchmarks for couriers, patient service centers and sales as a percent of revenue were not found, so the claim that 9% covers all commercial functions is unverified.

## 7. Legal and liability

1. **Medicare referral billing contradicts the structure.**
   - CMS manual ch. 16 §40.1 lets a referring lab bill for tests another lab performed only if:
     - it is in a rural hospital, or
     - the two are wholly owned by one another or by a third entity, or
     - it refers no more than 30% of its tests. (S) [CMS manual](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c16.pdf)
   - A 51/49 LLC that bills while the hospital core lab does 80-85% of testing meets none of these, unless the hospital is rural.
   - I found no disclosed structure where an LLC bills for tests done in the hospital's lab. The JVs I found build or use a JV-owned performing lab (Corewell's new lab, with billing mechanics in the interim undisclosed; ProMedica's JV core lab). Kootenai instead billed Labcorp as the reference lab, and Labcorp performs most of its own testing.
   - The fix pushes capital and equipment into the JV, or reduces the model to a management contract.
2. **Billing-agent pay.**
   - Medicare may pay an agent only if the agent's compensation "is not related in any way to the dollar amounts billed or collected". (S) [42 CFR 424.73](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/42/424.73)
   - That blocks a percent-of-collections fee where the operator receives payment. Paying into a provider-controlled account may avoid it (U).
3. **EKRA.**
   - Payments to third-party marketers are covered. Percent pay is not per se unlawful, but it falls outside the safe harbor. (S) [Frier Levitt](https://www.frierlevitt.com/articles/ninth-circuit-clarifies-permissible-marketing-compensation-under-ekra-laboratories-beware/)
   - An operator with sales staff paid by percent of revenue is the target profile. This binds only the Ninth Circuit.
4. **Payer enrollment cuts both ways.**
   - Anthem New Hampshire has excluded most hospital labs since 2010. Frisbie opened an independent lab company to get back in. (S) [Dark Report](https://www.darkintelligencegroup.com/the-dark-report/clinical-laboratory-trends/locked-out-of-payer-network-nh-hospital-opens-lab-company/)
   - UnitedHealthcare's July 2026 Preferred Lab Network lists Eurofins, Labcorp, Quest and specialty labs, with no hospital lab. (S) [UHC](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/resource-library/news/2026/preferred-lab-providers-july.html)
   - Re-enrolling at independent-lab rates opens networks but removes the premium. Hospital outpatient departments are paid about 3x independent labs, with 60% of spend. (S) [HCCI](https://healthcostinstitute.org/all-hcci-reports/price-markups-for-clinical-labs-employer-based-insurance-pays-hospital-outpatient-departments-3x-more-than-physician-offices-and-independent-labs-for-identical-tests/) Chi found nationals' net revenue per test about 20% below typical outreach.
5. **Gaps:** tax-exempt JV control rules (UBIT, Rev. Rul. 98-15), state laws and whether commercial payers copy the Medicare referral rule were not researched. Counsel is required.

## 8. Why-now

**Real**
- CMS preliminary 2027 rates average about 16% lower, with a 15% annual cap over 2027-29 and final rates due in November 2026. (S) [CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/preliminary-calendar-year-cy-2027-medicare-clinical-laboratory-fee-schedule-payment-rates)
- The sale wave is live: Labcorp's 13 deals in 2025, and Kaufman Hall expects acceleration into 2026. (S) [Vizient/Kaufman Hall](https://www.vizient.com/insights/articles/behind-the-boom-in-health-system-lab-transactions)

**Weak**
- PAMA cuts have been delayed repeatedly. The 2026 appropriations act moved them to 2027, and the lab industry is lobbying for the RESULTS Act again in the lame duck. (S, search summary) [MDDI](https://www.mddionline.com/medical-device-markets/quest-diagnostics-urges-congress-to-act-on-lab-payment-reform-as-cuts-loom)
- Quest's cash spent on acquisitions fell from $2.16B in 2024 to $101M in 2025. It shifted to Co-Lab and JVs.
- The shock favors whoever has cash and hubs.

## 9. Upside-case assumptions tested

| Assumption (gate) | Finding | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Core lab keeps 80-85% of testing in an operator-controlled LLC | Conflicts with CMS §40.1 unless the LLC performs the testing | Fails |
| 9% fee funds sales, couriers, patient centers, billing | Fee is 60-120% of the claimed savings pool; no cost benchmarks found | Unproven |
| Equity at 1.0-1.3x revenue | Verified comps are 2.4-2.7x | Fails (about 2x) |
| Two controlled JVs of about $45M each | Top-quartile programs (A) are the nationals' favorite targets; no precedent of a startup winning one | Weak |
| No independent operator | Orion/FMOL, Sonic JVs, TriCore, Quest 51/49, Atalan, advisory | Fails |
| Independent-rate enrollment preserves margin | Rates drop; RDL walked on that gap | Fails |
| Raise $50-90M untested | RDL had $250M committed and had stalled by 2015 | Weak |
| Why-now | Real but favors cash buyers | Partial |

## 10. Moat assessment (step 9)

| Moat | Quest/Labcorp | Regional independents (Orion, Sonic) | The pick |
|---|---|---|---|
| Network effects | Moderate (density) | Weak | Weak |
| Switching costs | Strong (Kootenai had a 5-year noncompete; EMR/billing lock-in) | Moderate | Moderate if contracts are long |
| Scale economies | Strong (hubs, couriers) | Moderate | Weak |
| Intangibles (payer contracts, licenses) | Strong | Moderate | Weak at start |

- Structural vulnerability: the buyer's best alternative is cash, and a successful operator is acquired by Labcorp (PAML).
- Durable advantage: none found. The "control" pitch is the only difference, and Orion and Sonic already offer it.

## 11. What would change my mind

1. Signed LOIs from 2+ systems with at least $30M of outreach to accept equity rather than cash.
2. A healthcare counsel opinion that a 51/49 LLC can bill without owning the performing lab.
3. A sponsor LOI for $120M+ at under 1.5x revenue.
4. One payer letter of intent for preferred network status.

If these cannot be had, the surviving variant is advisory-led. That is the boutique outcome the round-2 rules say to call dead.

## 12. Gaps

- Cost percentages for outreach couriers, patient service centers and sales.
- JV terms for Orion/FMOL.
- Atalan's current status.
- What share of outreach revenue is Medicare.
- Revenue of the divested CHS, Allina, OhioHealth and University Hospitals businesses.
- Sonic's US ROIC. I saw about 5.8% in a dated secondary analysis only.

objections: There is no open purchase order, and HHSC's own 2028-29 budget request already names who gets the new contracted beds. In the 9/4/2026 LAR, the capacity item (priority 4, about $256M a year) funds 'up to 286' contracted beds at Texas Behavioral Health Center, Montgomery County, Permian Basin and Doctors Hospital at Renaissance, and 'up to 132' beds at Victoria County and Baptist Beaumont. All of these were built with state grants. At the idea's own $697 a bed-day, 418 beds is about $100M a year (my arithmetic, civil/forensic split not stated). That is the whole Texas prize the pitch is chasing, and it is pre-assigned to six named local counterparties. The only new contract-bed ask is item 7, 'Strengthening Forensic Continuum': $46.3M for the biennium, covering 65 beds for extended forensic commitments (about $16M a year at $697, my arithmetic) plus diversion teams. That is a different, long-stay product, not initial restoration. The LAR also says 'contracted entities have expressed interest' in more beds, so incumbents are already queued. The 'Texas needs 600-1,000 more beds' premise has no budget line behind it.

The contract form the pitch assumes does not exist, and the form that does exist cannot be financed. The pitch says 'five-year availability-based contracts' and 'a bed pays for itself the moment it opens.' The only public HHSC instrument (HHS001336800001, 16 geriatric forensic beds) has an initial term ending 8/31/2025, extendable only 'at HHSC's sole discretion' to a 5-year maximum. It allows termination for convenience at any time in HHSC's sole discretion (s. 9.2). It states 'NO QUANTITY GUARANTEES' (s. 2.3) and a 'shall not exceed' spend cap. It funds 'only administrative and operational costs' and puts routine medical, psychiatric and discharge-medication costs inside the funding. It requires an annual budget summary and quarterly financial reports, and HHSC may offset payments. HHSC decides which patients you get, and only non-maximum-security patients. No lender or sale-leaseback investor funds modular units against a one-year, terminable, no-volume-guarantee, single-payer contract. The injunction does not change this. The judge said HHSC is not ordered to fund a project or sign a contract. Benchmarks are what HHSC 'believes in good faith' it can meet, there are no per-day fines, and the court found no intentional derogation. The state is appealing to the Fifth Circuit.

The buyer's revealed preference is to own the beds or grant the capital to local entities, and for-profit privatization has repeatedly been rejected. Texas has put more than $2.5B into 680+ state-owned beds and $239M in grants to counties and hospital districts. Washington bought Acadia's closed Tukwila hospital for $29.9M and hired 200+ state staff to run it. Georgia is spending $409M on a state hospital. California's pending list fell from 1,953 to 256 after about $2B of spending, and its jail-based beds are contracted with county sheriffs. Texas rejected GEO Care's Kerrville privatization bid in 2012. North Carolina rejected all bids for private forensic care and GEO abandoned its High Point hospital (both old precedents, so low weight on their own). HHSC's cheapest lever is not beds: its Forensic Support Teams removed 221 people from the waitlist and diverted another 119 from inpatient restoration between April 2025 and May 2026, and the LAR asks to expand them. Texas's list is down about 40% from its peak. Nationally, the median adult waitlist is 48 people across 24 states, so 'multi-state' means several separate state procurements. Each one is a different agency, a different statute and a 12-36 month cycle, aimed at demand that is already shrinking. The large stocks (Texas, Georgia, Colorado, Florida) are, respectively, pre-allocated, self-building, told by their own Special Master that contract beds should not be primary, and unfunded. Florida's gap analysis says 2,034 beds are needed by 2029, yet its requests are in the tens of millions, so need does not equal budget.

The price and margin cannot carry the capital or the risk. Forensic patients are essentially ineligible for Medicaid and Medicare (HHSC LAR), so the payer is state general revenue only, with no payer mix and a single counterparty. The one public Texas price of about $697 a bed-day must cover psychiatric and medical care. A Texas private operator said full cost is $700-900 a day and that it was 'losing money' at 90% full (Texas Tribune 2024, cited in the dossier). The product is squeezed between jail-based units at $171-$421 (Liberty, Harris County, Colorado) and a state hospital bed at $1,013. SB 528's required cost comparison, due 8/1/2027, hands HHSC a repricing benchmark. Contracted private hospitals also 'refuse forensic patients' while taking civil ones, per the expert testimony in the opinion. The sickest patients stay in state maximum-security units, so the contractable cohort is the lowest-acuity, lowest-priced slice. Capital is out of reach for a startup: a state build costs $2.1-2.4M a bed, grant-backed private beds carry $500-890k a bed of state money, and 414-640 beds needs $0.2-1.0B. The exit is also weak. Wellpath Recovery Solutions (about $425M revenue, 20+ years old) drew no qualifying outside bids and went to its lenders on a $395M credit bid, about 0.93x revenue. The market passed on a scaled forensic operator twice.

The go-to-market is lobbying plus an eligibility catch-22, with first revenue about 2029. HHSC's contract requires a licensed hospital with Joint Commission or CMS-deemed accreditation (s. 3.1.3). A 2022 HHSC solicitation snippet reportedly required current Joint Commission accreditation and 20+ beds (I could not open the page, so treat that as unverified). A new entrant is therefore ineligible until it runs an accredited hospital, which means buying one. Capacity is awarded through the Legislature and the Governor's grants to named local entities, so 'CAC' is political, not a sales funnel. The timeline is long. The Legislature convenes in January 2027 and funding starts 9/1/2027, then comes a solicitation, Contract Advisory Team review for contracts of $5M or more, licensing and build. Montgomery's state-financed 100-bed expansion took about 18 months from groundbreaking to patients on an already-licensed campus. Revenue is also concentrated: one agency per state is more than 90% of revenue, and it can terminate for convenience.

objections: NO BUYER HAS EVER ASKED TO TRANSFER OFF-SITE RISK, AND THE BEST-CASE STATES DID THE OPPOSITE. Virginia is the idea's ideal customer (off-site 27% of budget, $62M in FY2016). Its own 2016 DOC cost assessment (RD210) records: the first fully capitated vendor (CMS) quit after financial losses; Corizon used a 120-day exit in 2014 and forced an emergency contract that cost $6M a year more plus $14.2M of inpatient spend the DOC carved out and paid itself; in 2015 the DOC carved inpatient care OUT of the vendor contracts specifically to keep the Medicaid recoveries; and the legislature ordered a comparison of 'contractor full risk' vs 'Department assumes that risk'. Then in 2021 Virginia moved to take all care in-house. JLARC (2018) found no evidence contract facilities spend less on off-site services. Florida: Corizon walked from a $1.2B contract in year 3, saying it lost about $1M a month, after the legislature refused a rate increase. Oregon (the dossier's own 'pain' exhibit): the cause of the 17% weekly-spend jump was the DOC's own scheduling backlog, its fix was $4.9M and 18 in-house FTE, and it simply asked the legislature for $14.35M; nothing in the analysis points to outsourcing. Revealed preference is that DOCs keep off-site risk and Medicaid money. Nobody holds a budget line for 'risk transfer to a benefit manager', so the signer in the idea does not exist.

THE PRICE ANCHOR IS FREE, SO THE RISK PREMIUM HAS NOTHING TO BUY. The idea's savings (Medicare-based rates, Medicaid capture) are available by statute or admin action without a middleman: Virginia JLARC said a Medicare-based rate structure would save about $9M a year (roughly 15% of $62M) and just recommended piloting it; USMS is capped at Medicare by 18 U.S.C. 4006 and Heritage merely reprices; Florida caps non-contract hospitals at 110% of Medicare; NC auditors found it paid 467% of Medicaid rates and Medicaid inpatient billing saved about $10M a year (federal match 65% then, 90% for expansion adults now). A state is a better risk-bearer than a startup (diversified, can appropriate), so a PMPM that carries 5-8% margin, admin, and 15-20% of premium in reinsurance and surplus is negative expected value to the state unless utilization review (delay) generates the savings, which is exactly the lawsuit exposure. The only proven fee benchmark is small: DOJ OIG 25-096 shows USMS paid Heritage about $40M on roughly $620M of managed medical and drug spend over FY2018-24, about 6.5% or $5.7M a year, on the largest federal managed-care contract, running since 2007. $100M of fee revenue at that rate needs about $1.5-1.6B of managed spend, which is essentially the entire $1.1-1.8B reachable pool. As a risk-bearer, $100M of 'revenue' is premium and yields $5-8M of profit.

UNIT ECONOMICS FAIL ON VARIANCE, ADVERSE SELECTION AND CAPITAL BEFORE THE FIRST DOLLAR. Oregon's weekly off-site spend moved from $790K to $922K (+17%) in about six months, which is 2-3x a 5-8% margin. Nearly half of Virginia's $62M went to 179 people; people 65+ were 11% of Virginia's off-site cost. The DOCs that most want to outsource are the ones with suppressed historical claims (backlogs), so pricing off the run rate loses money in year one (the dossier's own estimate: about $6.9M a year lost on a $41M base). Every prior risk-taker in this market exited or failed: CMS (VA), Corizon (VA 2014, FL 2016), Armor (assignment for benefit of creditors 2023, $153.5M unsecured debt), Wellpath (Ch. 11), YesCare (May 2026). Buyers learned to distrust thin-capital risk takers, which is why the 2026 emergency awards went to whoever was already on paper. Capital needed: $15-20M surplus plus $4-11M working capital (dossier, A) to earn $5-8M a year at $100M of premium, a 3-5 year payback if no bad year occurs (A). The hospital discount depends on 5-10 year stable volume, but state contracts do not last: Michigan exited Wellpath two years early, Illinois dropped a 10-year $4B Wexford deal in July 2025, Alabama cancelled YesCare in 2026, Corizon cancelled in VA and FL. Volume is also unguaranteed (NJ DOC RFP: no minimum or maximum population guaranteed). Stop-loss is a negotiation too: the Maryland 2012 contract (search summary, unverified) had the state reimburse 50% of any admission above $25K, so incumbents with better data pushed the tail back to the state, shrinking what a risk-bearer can actually keep.

SALES CYCLE AND GO-TO-MARKET: ONE UNREPEATABLE, PROTESTABLE DECISION PER STATE PER FIVE YEARS, AND THE 'SHADOW BID' DOES NOT EXIST IN PROCUREMENT LAW. Observed cycles: Illinois has gone more than a year with no long-term contract and no RFP (90-day emergency contracts, then a one-year $507M Centurion deal, expiring 2027); Tennessee issued RFP 32901-31328-23 in Nov 2023, was set to award Wexford, Centurion protested, the state re-solicited, Wexford sued, and Centurion was extended in mid-2025; Maryland's award was made over a losing bidder's pending appeal; Alabama's earlier RFP was rescinded over undue-influence concerns and reissued, and its legislative committee held the roughly $1B contract; Alameda County staff put a county medical-services procurement at about 12 months including protest. Even the plain claims function drew BCBS of Nebraska, UMR (UnitedHealthcare), Falling Colors, Innovative Claims Strategies and Correctional Health Partners in Nebraska. The one live unbundled procurement (CDCR SD25-00019, 5+5 years, about 90,000 people) is network plus prior authorization with a state-designated TPA for claims and no risk transfer, so you would bid as a network manager at Heritage-type fees. This concept was already tried on the best-case state: in April 2012 Correctional Health Partners (Oregon's TPA) filed a letter of intent to become a prisoner CCO, alongside Centene and UnitedHealth; 14 years later Oregon still pays fee-for-service through a TPA (LFO, Jan 2026). Realistic volume: about 12-15 eligible states, each buying once per contract term, so roughly 3 eligible procurements a year nationally; at an assumed 20-30% win rate against incumbents (A), the '3 states plus 7 counties' first-ten list is a 4-6 year path to the first $100M of premium, and county deals pay $40-50 per claim (Polk, Limestone) or keep the tail themselves (a San Diego NaphCare cap of $20.6M a year with the county paying overages, unverified).

LICENSING AND LIABILITY CUT AGAINST THE PITCH. The idea says a PMPM carve-out is 'usually a vendor contract, not insurance'. Regulator positions I found say otherwise for a non-provider that keeps the loss on a fixed prepayment: Alaska Division of Insurance Bulletin B97-04 treats any entity assuming insurance risk as an insurer; a 1990 Maryland AG opinion treated fixed-capitation risk-takers as engaged in insurance (the pass-through TPA was not); a New York OGC opinion says an LLC capitated by a TPA for a self-funded entity must first become a licensed insurer (all from search summaries, so state-by-state confirmation is still needed). That puts certificate-of-authority and capital rules in the critical path in every target state. Liability does not transfer to you either: in the Fluvanna settlement Judge Moon held the DOC 'cannot delegate this responsibility away' despite a private vendor, so the state keeps its exposure while you add yours; courts let policy-based claims proceed against the contractor that denied outside referrals (Resendez v. Wexford), and the idea's selling point (UR that gates referrals) makes you the named gatekeeper at a time when professional-liability capacity is tightening. Add the hospital side: Nevada's Carson-Tahoe hospital stopped taking most Medicaid-eligible inmates in 2015 because Medicaid pays less than the prior plan, so Medicaid-rate pricing can break the network the whole product depends on, and Florida's HB 913 drafts sought to let DOC-contracted providers be paid above 110% of Medicare (final text unconfirmed), which suggests hospitals want a premium rather than a discount.

objections: The why-now is already stayed, and the dossier missed it. On 2026-09-18 a Fifth Circuit panel (Smith, Southwick, Douglas; No. 26-50619) granted Texas's motion for a stay pending appeal of the whole Ward v. Muth injunction, benchmarks and monitoring included. It found HHSC 'likely to succeed on the merits' on three separate grounds: Jackson v. Indiana probably does not apply to people not yet hospitalized; there is no fundamental right to a 21-day limit; and the waitlist 'is likely to pass' rational-basis review 'with flying colors.' The dossier says it found 'no ruling as of Oct 18', and the gate named the Fifth Circuit as the main risk, but that risk has already largely materialized. A footnote calls it a preliminary ruling by an administrative panel and leaves the final call to the merits panel, but the language pre-announces the outcome. With the stay, Texas has no legal duty to buy a single bed for at least a year and probably never. Every number in the plan (600 beds, 410 beds, 'a bed pays for itself') rested on that compulsion.

HHSC's own money request shows almost no uncommitted contract demand. The agency's FY2028-29 appropriations request was filed 2026-09-04, two months after the injunction. It never mentions the injunction. The only new contracted-forensic-bed ask is 65 beds for extended forensic commitments, inside exceptional item #7 of 38. Item #7's entire mental-health-community-hospitals allocation is $20.96M a year, and that also covers Forensic Support Team contracts. At the sourced $697-$880 a bed-day, 65 beds is about $16-20M a year of revenue for the whole pool. That is the ceiling for a new entrant, against the 410+ beds the $100M thesis needs. The larger item #4 ($256M a year) only operates capacity that already has named counterparties: the UT Southwestern-run Texas Behavioral Health Center in Dallas (292 beds), Montgomery County, Permian Basin, Doctors Hospital at Renaissance, and Victoria County/Baptist Beaumont (up to 286 + 132 beds). HHSC says 'contracted entities have expressed interest' in the 65 new beds, which means the incumbents. The state's cheaper lever is demand reduction: Forensic Support Teams removed 221 people from the waitlist and diverted 119 more. Its budgeted cost per occupied contracted bed falls from $831 (2026) to $658, $603 and $445 by 2029. That is a blended performance measure, not a rate, but the direction is bad.

A newcomer cannot sell the product, and the contract is not the 5-year availability contract the gate assumed. The one real HHSC forensic-bed contract (HHS001336800001, 16 beds, procured by RFQ) has these terms. The contractor must already be a Texas-licensed general or special hospital with Joint Commission or CMS-deemed accreditation (s. 3.1.3), so licensing and construction capital come before any contract. The initial term expired 2025-08-31, with extensions at HHSC's 'sole discretion' up to 5 years. HHSC may terminate for convenience 'at any time', effective on the date it specifies (s. 9.2). The contract is void with no prior notice and no liability if appropriations lapse (Art. III, s. 3.1). Spending is capped at $4.068M and HHSC can withhold or offset payments. Subcontracts need HHSC's written approval. The contractor bears routine medical, psychiatric and discharge-medication costs. On top of that, SB 528 (Health & Safety Code ch. 580, in force 9/2025) makes every contracting facility sign MOUs with the county, the municipality and the local mental health authority. It also requires annual public outcome reporting and a cost comparison against state hospitals, first due 2027-08-01. That adds three local veto players and a ready-made benchmark for squeezing rates. The only way in is as a subcontractor to a licensed incumbent, which is the Wellpath 'junior partner' model the dossier already flagged.

Capital, liability and exit value make this unfundable at venture terms. The state's grant-funded private beds carry $500-890k a bed of public money (Montgomery $50M for 100; DHR $85M for 100). State builds run $2.1-3.7M a bed. A 60-bed unit is roughly $14-15M a year of revenue with payroll due weeks before the first payment, under a contract that can be cancelled at will. The best-capitalized listed psychiatric operator shows the risk. Acadia paused de novo projects in November 2025 and still has about 3,000 beds in ramp-up chasing 70-75% occupancy. Its claims rose 186% in 2025, professional and general liability cost rose $61M, its self-insured retention went from $3M to $15M, and it has reserved $155M. A forensic population is the highest-liability cohort, and a startup cannot carry a $15M retention. Exit value is also poor: Wellpath's $425M-revenue behavioral division drew about 70 NDAs, no qualifying outside bids, and went to its lenders on a credit bid at roughly 0.93x revenue. The dossier's 8-12% EBITDA assumption also sits uneasily with the Texas private operator who said full cost is $700-900 a day against a $697 contract price.

The window closes before an entrant can open. Texas's own pipeline lands in 2026-27: Permian Basin +42 forensic (summer 2026), Texas Behavioral Health Center +292 (2026-27), Doctors Hospital at Renaissance +100 (half forensic, summer 2026) and Montgomery +100 forensic (winter 2027), on top of 680+ state-owned beds. The waitlist is already down about 40% from its December 2022 peak (2,711 to 1,628). A new entrant's sequence is: the 90th Legislature convenes in January 2027, funds start 2027-09-01, then a solicitation, then hospital licensure, then Joint Commission accreditation, then a ramp of up to 3 months. First revenue is therefore 2028-29, after the state's capacity is delivered and with the Fifth Circuit stay removing any compulsion. The hospital-licensure-plus-accreditation path also refutes the '6-12 months, modular' claim, as the dossier found. Texas is the only market sized for this. Colorado's decree runs only to 2027 and its Special Master says contract beds 'should never be the primary strategy'. Washington, Georgia and California are building their own capacity. The result is a build-out spike that incumbents and grant-funded shells absorb, not a durable multi-state operator business.

I would reverse the fatal call if all of the following showed up.
1. The Fifth Circuit stay is vacated, or a merits panel affirms a 21-day (or similarly binding) admission requirement. As things stand, a rational-basis ruling for Texas would remove the legal compulsion for Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi at once.
2. The 90th Legislature appropriates for the 2028-29 biennium at least 300 contracted forensic beds that are not already assigned to named grant recipients (Dallas Texas Behavioral Health Center, Montgomery, Permian Basin, Doctors Hospital at Renaissance, Victoria/Beaumont). HHSC then runs an open competitive solicitation that a new operator can win.
3. A signed HHSC (or other state) contract shows a firm term of 3 years or more with availability or take-or-pay payment, no termination for convenience on short notice, and a per-day rate of $800 or more with operator margin of 15% or more. A Public Information Act pull of all private inpatient restoration contracts would show this, and it would also reveal whether the 65-bed ask is real money.
4. A licensed, Joint Commission-accredited hospital agrees to hold the license and subcontract the beds, HHSC pre-approves the subcontract in writing, and a county or state grant covers the build. That would remove the chicken-and-egg capital problem, though it would make the company a manager that keeps only a thin fee.
5. A second state issues a funded RFP for 200 or more beds open to private operators, with no in-house build competing with it. That would show the model is multi-state and not a Texas one-off."

objections: The exact structure was already tried by states, failed, and was reversed. Virginia's own 2016 cost report (RD210) says its first comprehensive vendor (CMS) had 'all financial risk' under capitation and 'terminated the contract after suffering financial losses'. Corizon took 17 facilities on full capitation in 2013 and used its 120-day termination right in 2014, forcing an emergency contract. The latest Virginia contracts then carved inpatient care out of capitation and put that risk back on DOC, which also collects the Medicaid inpatient reimbursement. Virginia's third-party administrator for claims, inpatient utilization review and negotiated pricing has been Anthem BCBS since 2011, and VCU Health handles about 77% of off-site care under state memoranda of agreement. The pattern repeats in 2026: Alabama (YesCare to NaphCare), Illinois (Wexford to a one-year Centurion deal), Kansas (to VitalCore), and Florida's cost-plus contract. Buyers hold the risk or swap full-service vendors. The only piece they buy from third parties is the fee-based administrator layer (Anthem, Heritage, five bidders for Nebraska's claims RFP), which is a $10-35M business, not $100M. The risk-bearing layer adds nothing a state wants, because a state budget pools this variance better than a startup can and keeps the Medicaid match.

The unit economics and capital do not close, and the obvious strategic backer already left. The idea targets 5-8% margin on gross premium. Observed variance is far larger: Wellpath quit Georgia citing more than $30M of unanticipated costs in one year and left hospital arrears of $75.6M. Its court filings reportedly show about $40M of negative gross profit on the Michigan and Georgia contracts (secondary source). Michigan hospitals say $35M+ went unpaid under a 50/50 risk-share structure. Oregon's off-site backlog pushed weekly spend up 17%, and 179 people drove nearly half of Virginia's $62M. Georgia's contract was effectively nine one-year agreements, and Illinois is on a one-year deal, so a new entrant cannot amortize hospital-contract investment over the 5-10 years the 'earned secret' needs. The DOC holds the claims history and the entrant does not, which is adverse selection. Centene's own 8-K shows it divested Centurion in January 2023 after a $259M impairment, and HealthSmart (a TPA) after a $36M impairment. The idea file and gate still call Centurion a Centene subsidiary. Liability and stop-loss capacity is thin: a prospective bidder in Catawba County, NC (March 2026) said it could not find any carrier for a $5M umbrella on correctional medical risk, and the county refused to lower the limit. I found only public pools for catastrophic inmate medical cover (PRISM at $1M per inmate), and no stop-loss pricing for a vendor-level capitation.

The credibility and timing gap is too wide for an entrant. After $75.6M in unpaid Georgia claims (Wellstar alone $11.9M) and $35M+ in Michigan, hospitals and DOCs will treat a new risk-bearing intermediary as the weakest payer in the chain. They will want state payment or collateral, which removes the float that makes '15-day pay buys the discount' work. Per Pew-era data and the dossier, the biggest off-site spenders are in-house or university-model states, where the state hospital is the counterparty (VCU 77% in Virginia) and a private middleman cannot reprice it. Entry requirements stack up: a TPA license per state, URAC accreditation (sources give roughly 6-12 months from scratch), contracts with every local hospital (Polk's notice), and past-performance scoring in a post-collapse market that rewards balance sheets. A shadow bid in 90 days does not produce a contract. The realistic first revenue is a 2028-29 rebid, after this year's emergency awards (NaphCare 24 months, Centurion, VitalCore) have locked in a cycle.

The core value proposition has a logic flaw and a liability trap. The pitch says incumbents lose because the on-site vendor is both gatekeeper and payer. But a fixed per-member-per-month price makes the carve-out firm the same thing: margin equals PMPM minus approved claims, so every delayed or denied referral raises profit. 'Independent utilization review' with published timelines is a self-policed SLA. Plaintiffs already plead collegial review and off-site referral policies as the Monell 'policy' against vendors (Howell, Dean v. Wexford, Reed v. Wexford discovery orders), and I found no ruling that shields a utilization-review vendor. Virginia's court ruling (Judge Moon, Fluvanna) says the agency 'cannot delegate' its constitutional duty, so the DOC keeps the liability anyway and will not pay a premium to pretend otherwise. The Medicaid angle also cuts against the model. In expansion states the largest cost (inpatient) already goes to Medicaid at the state's lowest rates, shrinking the premium base. The Florida legislature's own benchmark for DOC provider payment was the Medicaid allowable rate, below the Medicare-plus network this idea sells.

The dossier's 'statute is the free substitute' claim is wrong on the key example, but the correction does not help the idea. HB 913, as enacted (Ch. 2026-111), concerns inmate welfare trust fund deductions and has no payment cap. The Florida Hospital Association report says the original bill capped provider payment at the Medicaid rate unless the provider contracted with DOC, that FHA testified against it, and that the sponsor 'remove[d] all compensation provisions'. Only county-specific caps (Jefferson, Lake, Indian River, and Polk per a third-party tracker) passed, at 110% of Medicare for non-contract providers. So hospitals organize effectively against rate benchmarks and will defend their pricing power. Hospital finances are tightening ahead of the 2027 Medicaid cuts (bad debt up 8% year over year per Kaufman Hall; Sentara seeking +6.2% from Anthem against a 1% cut offered), which pushes the other way from willingness to accept Medicare-plus for one state's inmate volume. A state's inmate volume is a rounding error to a health system, while the DOC's own sovereign 15-day payment promise needs no intermediary.
